intervention_name: Gender-based IPV prevention program (unit-based curriculum)

population.sample_size_detail: 200 experimental, 144 control

intervention.description: 3 units (gender stereotypes, gender-based IPV, socio-emotional skills), 2 sessions/week for 3 months, delivered in classroom

study_design_full: Quasi-experimental (non-randomized experimental vs control group, pre/post)

effect.direction: Mixed - effective on most attitude/stereotype outcomes, not effective on self-esteem or emotional intelligence
worked_for: Male and female gender stereotypes
Gender stereotypes in romantic relationships
Attitudes toward physical violence and physical violence against women
Acceptance of peer aggression (weak, strong, against men, against women)
Affective empathy
did_not_work_for: Self-esteem
Emotional intelligence
Cognitive empathy

key_message: A short classroom curriculum addressing gender stereotypes, IPV, and socio-emotional skills can shift attitudes and reduce acceptance of violence in children as young as 7-9, before they reach the 10-14 age range where dating and partner violence risk rises - though it did not move self-esteem or emotional intelligence, and effects on aggression acceptance were stronger for boys.
limitations: Quasi-experimental design (non-randomized); groups assigned by class scheduling availability
Inconsistent teacher engagement interrupted some sessions
Low family/parent involvement despite intended relevance
Relies on self-report scales, some risk of social desirability bias
No follow-up measurement beyond immediate post-test (no medium/long-term data)
Single school, single country - limited generalizability

intervention_name: Community mobilisation for domestic violence prevention (SNEHA-TARA)

population.age_range: Women 15-49 years (survey population); men, women, and young people participated in groups
population.sex: Mixed (women's, men's, and youth groups; primary outcome measured in women)
population.sample_size_detail: 48 clusters of ~500 households; 3606 women (intervention) and 3592 women (control) in the post-intervention survey

intervention.description: Community mobilisation over 3 years of exposure (delivered 2018-2023, delayed by COVID-19): women's, men's, and youth peer-education groups; volunteer "sanginis" who identify and support survivors; caseworkers providing crisis, legal, and psychosocial support.
intervention.duration: 3 years of exposure (implemented over ~4-5 years including a COVID-19 pause)

study_design_full: Two-arm, pragmatic, theory-driven, cluster-randomised controlled trial; 48 clusters, 1:1 allocation

effect.direction: No significant reduction in measured population prevalence of violence, but a large, significant increase in disclosure and access to support
worked_for: Disclosure of violence to support services (more than doubled: 9.3% control vs 20.9% intervention; adjusted OR 2.75, 95% CI 1.73-4.37)
Over 4000 survivors identified and supported through the programme
80%+ of women who met a caseworker reported reduced violence within 6 months
did_not_work_for: Population-level prevalence of physical or sexual domestic violence (adjusted OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.62-1.16 - not statistically significant)
Population-level prevalence of gender-based household maltreatment (adjusted OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.66-1.33 - not statistically significant)
Community attitudes to violence, gender inequality, and bystander support (trended favourably but not statistically significant)
Population mental health/wellbeing (no measurable difference)

key_message: A well-implemented, high-fidelity community mobilisation programme (women's/men's/youth groups plus trained volunteer responders) can dramatically increase disclosure of domestic violence and connect survivors to support - but did not produce a statistically significant reduction in population-level violence prevalence within the trial period. This is an important caution for practitioners: strong implementation and individual-level impact does not guarantee measurable population-level prevalence change, and attitude/norm change may not be a precondition for people to take protective action.
limitations: COVID-19 paused in-person activities for ~13 months, disrupting a planned midline survey and complicating interpretation
Trial was powered to detect a 6% prevalence difference; observed risk differences were smaller than this
Increased awareness and confidence in intervention communities may have increased disclosure in surveys, narrowing the measured gap between arms
Binary violence measures may not capture changes in severity or frequency of violence
Consent-seeking from cluster gatekeepers may have selected against the highest-violence localities
Two participant suicides occurred in intervention clusters during the trial (investigated, not attributed to the intervention)

intervention_name: COMPASS life skills and safe spaces programme

population.sample_size_detail: 457 intervention, 462 control (wait-list); Sudanese and South Sudanese refugee girls in Ethiopian camps

intervention.description: Weekly life skills sessions (30 total) delivered by trained young female refugee mentors in "safe spaces," plus 8 monthly discussion sessions for caregivers, covering communication, GBV awareness, and sexual/reproductive health.

study_design_full: Two-arm, single-blinded, wait-list, cluster-randomised controlled trial across 62 clusters

effect.direction: No significant effect on the primary violence outcome, but significant positive effects on protective attitudes and social support
worked_for: Attitudes toward appropriate age of marriage (adjusted OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.07-3.28) and age of first child (aOR 2.04, 95% CI 1.25-3.34)
Having same-age friends (aOR 1.71) and a trusted non-family female adult (aOR 2.00)
Reduced child marriage among the subgroup already married/cohabiting at baseline (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.34-0.95)
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome: any past-year sexual violence (adjusted OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.59-1.57 - not significant)
Physical violence, emotional violence, and transactional sex
Feelings of safety at home, school, or in the community

key_message: In a refugee camp setting, a life-skills and safe-spaces programme for adolescent girls did not measurably reduce direct exposure to violence within 12 months, but it did shift protective attitudes (later marriage/childbearing) and expand girls' social support networks - markers considered earlier steps on the causal pathway to violence reduction. This echoes a pattern seen in other studies on this platform: individual and attitudinal change can occur even when population-level violence outcomes don't shift within a trial's timeframe.
limitations: All outcomes self-reported, with risk of disclosure and social desirability bias (partially mitigated via audio computer-assisted self-interview)
Programme roll-out was delayed, so the primary outcome's 12-month reference period overlapped with intervention delivery rather than fully following it
Violence measures were binary (any exposure) rather than measuring frequency or severity
Potential spillover/contamination between intervention and control girls sharing the same camps
A planned longer-term follow-up round was not possible due to funding limitations

intervention_name: Girl Empower (GE / GE+): mentoring, life skills, and cash transfer

population.sample_size_detail: 84 villages, three arms (control/GE/GE+); 1176 analyzed at 24-month follow-up

intervention.description: 32 weekly life-skills sessions with trained female mentors in safe spaces, 8 monthly caregiver discussion groups, and individual girl savings accounts ($2/month). GE+ variant adds a cash incentive to caregivers for girls' attendance (~$1.25/session).
intervention.duration: 9 months of programming (Feb-Nov 2016), assessed at 24-month follow-up

study_design_full: Parallel, three-arm (control, GE, GE+), cluster-randomised controlled trial at the village level

effect.direction: No significant effect on sexual or physical violence despite very high programme fidelity, but significant sustained gains in gender attitudes, life skills, and sexual/reproductive health
worked_for: Gender attitudes (GE: 0.206 SD, p<0.05; GE+: 0.228 SD, p<0.05)
Life skills - HIV knowledge, financial literacy, condom knowledge (GE: 0.224 SD, p<0.05; GE+: 0.289 SD, p<0.01)
Sexual and reproductive health - later marriage, fewer partners, safer sex (GE: 0.244 SD, p<0.01; GE+: 0.372 SD, p<0.01 - roughly 50% stronger with the added cash transfer)
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome: sexual violence index (no significant effect for GE or GE+)
Physical violence
Schooling and psychosocial wellbeing (small, not statistically significant)
Protective factors: social capital and caregivers' gender norms/attitudes were not affected

key_message: Even with very high attendance (girls attended ~28 of 32 sessions) and rigorous trial design, a life-skills, mentoring, and small-cash-transfer programme for girls aged 13-14 did not reduce their exposure to sexual or physical violence over 24 months - despite producing real, sustained gains in gender attitudes, life skills, and sexual/reproductive health. This is the third study on this platform showing the same pattern: individual-level attitude and knowledge change is achievable, but doesn't reliably translate into measured reductions in violence within a study's timeframe. Adding a modest cash incentive for caregivers roughly doubled the effect on sexual/reproductive health outcomes specifically.
limitations: All outcomes self-reported; baseline violence prevalence was extremely high (37% ever experienced sexual violence, 94.8% reported physical violence during the 24-month study period), raising questions about measurement sensitivity as well as true exposure
The trial could not isolate the individual contribution of the cash transfer versus the mentoring programme (no cash-only arm)
Well powered to detect effects on the seven composite indices, but not on individual sub-components
The GE+ cash incentive ended up larger than originally planned due to a study implementation error, complicating clean interpretation of the "plus cash" effect
Set in a specific post-Ebola, post-conflict context (rural Liberia) that may limit generalizability elsewhere

intervention_name: No Means No (COVID-adapted): empowerment-based self-defense program

population.sex: Girls (girls-only arm) and girls plus boys (co-ed arm)
population.sample_size_detail: 15 schools cluster-randomised 1:1:1 to a girls-only intervention arm, a girls-plus-boys intervention arm, or control; individual participant count not confirmed in available secondary sources

intervention.description: COVID-adapted 'No Means No' empowerment-based self-defense curriculum using experiential learning (e.g. role play) to build practical skills for recognizing and resisting sexual assault situations, delivered either to girls only or to girls and boys separately within the same schools
intervention.duration: School-based delivery; outcomes assessed at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months

study_design_full: Hybrid type-1 effectiveness-implementation, three-arm, cluster-randomised controlled trial across 15 schools (girls-only intervention vs girls+boys intervention vs control, 1:1:1 allocation)

effect.direction: No statistically significant reduction in the primary outcome (past-year sexual violence exposure, including harassment or rape) in either intervention arm compared to control at 12 months
worked_for: Demonstrated feasibility of delivering and evaluating a COVID-adapted empowerment self-defense curriculum via a hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster trial across 15 schools despite pandemic-related disruption
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome: past-year sexual violence exposure (harassment or rape) among girls - no statistically significant difference between either intervention arm and control

key_message: A COVID-adapted version of the widely used 'No Means No' empowerment self-defense curriculum did not produce a statistically significant reduction in South African girls' past-year exposure to sexual violence after 12 months, in either the girls-only or mixed-sex delivery format. This is a notable caution alongside more positive results from earlier in-person 'No Means No' trials in Kenya and Malawi: pandemic-driven adaptations to delivery format and intensity may have diluted impact on the primary violence outcome, even where the trial itself was delivered successfully.
limitations: COVID-19-adapted delivery and timeline may differ meaningfully from the original in-person 'No Means No' model evaluated in earlier Kenya and Malawi trials
Primary outcome relies on girls' self-reported experiences of sexual violence, with possible disclosure and social desirability bias
Trial conducted in a single city (Gqeberha) - generalizability to other South African or regional contexts is uncertain
Hybrid effectiveness-implementation design balances feasibility/implementation questions alongside effectiveness, which may affect statistical power for detecting the primary outcome

intervention_name: iCAN Plan 4 Safety: tailored online safety and health decision aid

population.sample_size_detail: 462 Canadian women who had experienced recent intimate partner violence, randomised to a tailored interactive version or a static non-tailored version of the online tool

intervention.description: Interactive, tailored online safety and health decision aid (iCAN Plan 4 Safety) that generates personalized safety planning content based on a woman's own risk and context, compared against a static, non-tailored version of the same tool
intervention.duration: Self-directed online use; outcomes measured at baseline and 3, 6, and 12 months via online surveys

study_design_full: Double-blind, two-arm randomised controlled trial (tailored interactive tool vs static non-tailored tool)

effect.direction: Women in both the tailored and non-tailored arms improved significantly over time on depressive symptoms and PTSD symptoms (both p<.001) and on all secondary outcomes, but the tailored version showed no significant advantage over the static, non-tailored version
worked_for: Depressive symptoms - improved over time in both arms (p<.001)
PTSD symptoms - improved over time in both arms (p<.001)
Secondary outcomes (helpfulness of safety actions, confidence in safety planning, mastery, social support, coercive control, decisional conflict) - improved over time in both arms
did_not_work_for: Tailoring/personalization did not produce significantly better outcomes than the static, non-tailored version on any primary or secondary measure

key_message: Both a tailored, interactive online safety-planning tool and a simpler static version of it were followed by sustained improvements in depression, PTSD symptoms, and safety-related outcomes for Canadian women experiencing intimate partner violence over 12 months - but personalizing the tool's content added no measurable extra benefit over the plain version. This suggests that simply providing structured, accessible online safety and health information/support may be the active ingredient, not the sophistication of tailoring, which has cost and complexity implications for how such digital tools are built and scaled.
limitations: No true no-intervention control arm - both arms received an online tool, so overall improvement cannot be fully attributed to either version versus no support at all
All outcomes self-reported via online survey, with potential attrition and social desirability bias
Sample restricted to women who could access and were willing to use an online tool, which may limit generalizability to women with less digital access or literacy
Single-country (Canada) high-income setting; applicability to lower-resource contexts unclear

intervention_name: Group programme for male perpetrators of intimate partner violence, with parallel partner support

population.sex: Mixed (male perpetrators plus their current/ex female partners)
population.sample_size_detail: 36 men (22 randomised to the intervention group programme, 14 to usual care) plus 15 current/ex-partners (39% of eligible partners) providing one-to-one support and outcome data

intervention.description: 23-week group programme for male perpetrators of intimate partner violence in heterosexual relationships, with an average of three individual one-to-one sessions for men, plus separate one-to-one support for their current or ex female partners
intervention.duration: 23 weeks group programming; outcomes assessed via self-report at 9 months

study_design_full: Pragmatic, individually randomised pilot and feasibility trial with an integrated qualitative study, conducted at one site (three local-authority areas) in England

effect.direction: This was a feasibility trial, not powered to detect effects on abuse outcomes; it found it was feasible to recruit, randomise, and retain both male perpetrators and female victim/survivors and to collect self-reported outcome data, with participants reporting positive engagement
worked_for: Recruitment, randomisation, and retention of both male perpetrators and female (ex-)partners were feasible - 67% (24/36) of men and 80% (12/15) of women completed 9-month self-report questionnaires
Men who completed all or most of the programme gave positive qualitative feedback and reported behaviour change
Trial design and procedures were judged acceptable to participants
did_not_work_for: Not powered or designed to establish whether the programme actually reduces intimate partner violence - a full-scale effectiveness trial would be needed

key_message: This UK pilot showed that a randomised trial of a perpetrator-focused group programme - paired with dedicated support for (ex-)partners - is feasible to run: recruitment, randomisation, and follow-up all worked well, and men who engaged reported positive change. But as a feasibility study it cannot say whether the programme reduces abuse; that requires a larger, adequately powered effectiveness trial, which the authors recommend as a next step.
limitations: Small sample (36 men, 15 partners) explicitly not powered to detect effectiveness on violence outcomes
Only 39% of eligible partners consented to take part, and partner data relies on their own self-report
Single site (one area, three local authorities) in England limits generalizability
No blinding of participants or intervention facilitators to allocation (not possible for a group-format behavioural intervention)

intervention_name: MAISHA: participatory gender-training social empowerment intervention (microfinance-linked)

population.age_range: Adult women in group-based microfinance loan schemes
population.sample_size_detail: 66 pre-existing microfinance loan groups in Mwanza City randomised in blocks of six (33 intervention groups, n=544 women; 33 control groups, n=505 women)

intervention.description: 10-session participatory gender-training curriculum ('MAISHA') delivered to women in their existing microfinance loan groups, addressing gender norms, communication, and economic/social empowerment to prevent intimate partner violence; control groups were wait-listed for the intervention after the trial

study_design_full: Cluster-randomised controlled trial; 66 pre-existing microfinance loan groups randomised in blocks of six to intervention or wait-list control

effect.direction: Women in the intervention arm were less likely to report past-year physical or sexual IPV (23% vs 27%; adjusted OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47-1.01; p=0.056, narrowly missing conventional significance), and significantly less likely to report physical IPV alone (aOR 0.64, 95% CI 0.41-0.99; p=0.043); effects on attitudes accepting of IPV were strong and highly significant
worked_for: Physical intimate partner violence alone (aOR 0.64, 95% CI 0.41-0.99; p=0.043)
Attitudes accepting of intimate partner violence (aOR 0.45, 95% CI 0.34-0.61; p<0.0001)
Belief that IPV is a private matter (aOR 0.51, 95% CI 0.32-0.81; p=0.005)

A companion trial (CRT01) restricted to pre-existing microfinance groups found stronger effects on physical IPV among women who were younger, more financially independent, and without prior physical IPV
did_not_work_for: Composite past-year physical-or-sexual-IPV outcome fell just short of conventional statistical significance (aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47-1.01; p=0.056)
Belief that IPV should be tolerated - borderline, not significant (aOR 0.68, 95% CI 0.45-1.01; p=0.055)
A related trial (CRT02) delivering the same curriculum to newly formed groups without a pre-existing microfinance link found no impact on physical IPV, overall or in subgroups

key_message: A 10-session participatory gender-training curriculum delivered to women already participating in microfinance loan groups in Tanzania was associated with less physical intimate partner violence and a strong shift away from attitudes that excuse or normalise IPV, though the composite physical-or-sexual-violence outcome narrowly missed conventional statistical significance. A companion trial found the same curriculum had no effect when delivered to newly formed groups without a pre-existing microfinance relationship - suggesting that combining gender-transformative training with real economic ties/group cohesion, not curriculum content alone, may be what drives impact.
limitations: Composite primary outcome (any physical or sexual IPV) did not reach conventional statistical significance (p=0.056), so findings are suggestive rather than conclusive on the primary endpoint

Effectiveness appears contingent on delivery through pre-existing microfinance groups; a companion trial in newly formed, non-microfinance groups found no effect, limiting generalizability of the standalone curriculum
Outcomes are self-reported experiences of a highly sensitive topic, with potential for social desirability and disclosure bias
Single city (Mwanza) in Tanzania - generalizability to other settings uncertain

intervention_name: SHARE: integrated intimate partner violence and HIV prevention intervention

population.age_range: Adults (married/cohabiting couples in an existing HIV research cohort)
population.sample_size_detail: 4 intervention clusters and 7 control clusters drawn from the existing Rakai Community Cohort Study; individual-level enrollment numbers not confirmed in available secondary sources

intervention.description: Community-level mobilisation to shift attitudes, social norms, and behaviours around intimate partner violence, layered onto standard HIV testing/counselling services, plus screening and brief intervention promoting safe HIV-status disclosure among women (the SHARE Project)
intervention.duration: Baseline survey Feb 2005-Jun 2006; two follow-up survey rounds through Dec 2009

study_design_full: Analysis of an intervention nested within an existing cluster-randomised cohort (Rakai Community Cohort Study); 4 intervention vs 7 control clusters

effect.direction: Exposure to SHARE was associated with reductions in some forms of IPV against women and in overall HIV incidence, plausibly via reduced forced sex and increased disclosure of HIV status; effects were not uniform across all forms of IPV or subgroups
worked_for: Some forms of intimate partner violence against women (reductions associated with intervention exposure)
Overall HIV incidence in the intervention population

Participant engagement - 77% of the intervention population were aware of SHARE, of whom 73% participated in activities, and two-thirds of participants felt it influenced their own behaviour around IPV
did_not_work_for: Effects were not uniform across all forms of IPV or all subgroups; exact effect sizes for each individual violence outcome were not confirmed in available secondary sources - consult the primary article for full figures

key_message: By layering a community mobilisation and safe-disclosure intervention onto an existing HIV research and service infrastructure in rural Uganda, the SHARE project was associated with reductions in some forms of intimate partner violence against women alongside reduced HIV incidence - suggesting IPV prevention and HIV prevention can be meaningfully combined rather than run as separate programmes. The authors argued this ecological approach could be adopted as part of standard care within other HIV programmes in sub-Saharan Africa.
limitations: Nested within a pre-existing HIV cohort study rather than a purpose-built trial, with clusters unevenly split (4 intervention vs 7 control)
Precise effect sizes and confidence intervals for individual violence outcomes were not confirmed in the secondary sources available for this summary
Self-reported IPV and HIV-status disclosure are both sensitive to social desirability and recall bias
The same research group has separately discussed the ethical and methodological complexities of randomising exposure to a violence-prevention intervention within an existing cohort

intervention_name: IMpower (girls) + 50:50 (boys): empowerment, self-defense, and gender-norms curriculum

population.sex: Girls (outcomes measured); boys received a parallel gender-norms curriculum (50:50) alongside them
population.sample_size_detail: 28 primary schools in Nairobi informal settlements (14 intervention, 14 standard-of-care control); 3147 girls surveyed in intervention schools and 2539 in control schools (open-cohort, cross-sectional surveys at baseline and ~9-month follow-up)

intervention.description: Six 2-hour classroom sessions delivered by instructors from the same informal settlements: girls received IMpower (empowerment, gender relations, and self-defense skills), boys received 50:50 (healthy gender norms), delivered in parallel at the same schools; control schools received a health and hygiene curriculum
intervention.duration: 6 sessions; outcomes assessed at baseline and ~9 months later

study_design_full: Cluster-randomised, matched-pairs, parallel trial; 28 primary schools matched on school size, academic performance, and other covariates before randomisation to intervention or standard-of-care control (14 pairs)

effect.direction: Significant reduction in past-year sexual assault (risk difference -3.7 percentage points, p=0.03, 95% CI 0.4-8.0) and significant increase in generalised self-efficacy (+0.19 on a 1-4 scale, p=0.0004) in intervention schools relative to control
worked_for: Past-year sexual assault - reduced from a baseline of ~7.3% (risk difference -3.7 percentage points; p=0.03, 95% CI 0.4-8.0%)
Generalised self-efficacy scale (GSES) - increased by 0.19 points on a 1-4 scale (p=0.0004, 95% CI 0.08-0.39)
Disclosure of sexual assault at follow-up trended higher in the intervention group (65%) than control (52%, p=0.051), though this was an exploratory rather than primary outcome
did_not_work_for: Distribution of who girls disclosed their assault to (boyfriend, relative, friend, authority figure) showed no meaningful shift between intervention and control - though this was an exploratory, not primary, outcome

key_message: In a large cluster-randomised trial across 28 Nairobi informal-settlement primary schools, a parallel empowerment/self-defense curriculum for girls (IMpower) alongside a gender-norms curriculum for boys (50:50) produced a statistically significant reduction in past-year sexual assault and a significant increase in girls' self-efficacy after just six 2-hour sessions. This is a notable positive counterpoint within the empowerment self-defense literature on this platform - the same intervention family's COVID-adapted South African replication (Hartmann et al. 2025) did not find a significant effect on its primary violence outcome, suggesting delivery intensity, age group, or context may matter for whether these programmes work.
limitations: All outcomes self-reported via unlinked, ballot-box-style classroom surveys with no individual identifiers, limiting ability to track individual-level change over time
Course instructors also administered the outcome surveys to their own students, creating potential demand effects/social desirability bias, especially in the intervention arm
Relatively short follow-up period (about 9 months)
Possible cross-contamination between geographically close intervention and control schools/communities, despite using distance in the matching/randomisation
Two schools were lost to follow-up after randomisation, and the open-cohort design meant individual students were not tracked between baseline and follow-up

intervention_name: Right To Play Positive Child and Youth Development Programme (play-based life-skills)

population.sex: Mixed (delivered in single-sex schools: 20 boys' schools, 20 girls' schools)
population.sample_size_detail: 40 single-sex public schools in Hyderabad, Pakistan (20 intervention, 20 control); 1752 grade 6 students enrolled (929 intervention, 823 control), 91% retained at 24 months, no school dropout

intervention.description: Two-year play-based life-skills programme (Right To Play's Positive Child and Youth Development Programme): biweekly structured game led by a trained coach, followed by 30 minutes of critical reflection and discussion

study_design_full: Two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial; 40 single-sex public schools (20 intervention, 20 control)

effect.direction: Significant reductions in peer violence victimization, perpetration, and depression for both boys and girls at 24 months, with substantially larger effects for girls
worked_for: Peer violence victimization - girls: 58.5% reduction (intervention) vs 21.3% (control); boys: 33.3% vs 27.8%
Peer violence perpetration - girls: 55.6% reduction vs 27.6% (control); boys: 25.3% vs 11.1%
Depression scores - girls: 9.5% reduction vs 5.6% (control); boys: 7.2% vs 4.8%
Gender attitudes became significantly less patriarchal in the intervention arm, with a greater shift for girls
Corporal punishment at school and physical punishment at home reported significantly less often in the intervention arm, with a greater reduction for girls
Exploratory outcomes (experiencing hunger, witnessing fighting between father figures, witnessing mother being beaten at home) were significantly less common in the intervention arm for both sexes
did_not_work_for: Self-assessed school performance score - no significant change
Days of school missed in the past 4 weeks - increased in both arms, not significantly different between them
Proportion of children promised in marriage - trended favourably but not statistically significant

key_message: A two-year, biweekly play-based life-skills programme delivered in Pakistani public schools produced significant reductions in peer violence victimization, perpetration, and depression for both boys and girls - with notably larger effects for girls (e.g. a 58.5% reduction in victimization vs 21.3% in control, compared to 33.3% vs 27.8% for boys). The programme also shifted gender attitudes and reduced corporal/physical punishment exposure, again with stronger effects for girls, and reduced children's exposure to witnessing violence at home - suggesting that broad life-skills empowerment programming in early adolescence can have gendered protective effects that go beyond its immediate peer-violence target.
limitations: All outcome measures were self-reported over a 'last four weeks' recall window
Coaches were not blinded to primary outcomes, and the independent research team's closer-than-usual oversight of sessions may have strengthened programme adherence beyond typical delivery conditions
Individual-level intervention dose/attendance was not analysed
Girls in the intervention arm had slightly higher baseline scores for victimization, depression, and corporal punishment than control-arm girls, requiring baseline adjustment

intervention_name: Gender Dialogue Groups added to an economic empowerment savings program (VSLA + GDG)
source: BMC International Health and Human Rights 13:46

population.age_range: Adult women (18+) and their male partners
population.sex: Women only (primary outcome); male partners also participated in the gender dialogue sessions
population.sample_size_detail: 24 rural villages randomised (village-level, non-blinded RCT); 981 partnered women enrolled, 934 (95.2%) completed baseline and endline data collection

intervention.description: Addition of 'Gender Dialogue Groups' (8 sessions targeting women and their male partners on gender norms) to an existing Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) economic-empowerment group savings program, compared to VSLA savings alone
intervention.duration: 8 sessions; study conducted 2010-2012, assessed at endline

study_design_full: Two-armed, non-blinded, village-randomised controlled pilot trial (VSLA + Gender Dialogue Groups vs VSLA only); 24 villages

effect.direction: No significant reduction in the primary outcome (past-year physical and/or sexual IPV) in intent-to-treat analysis, but significant reductions in economic abuse and acceptance of wife-beating; per-protocol analysis among higher-attendance couples showed a significant reduction in physical IPV
worked_for: Economic abuse (intent-to-treat): OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.25-0.60, p<0.0001
Acceptance of wife-beating (intent-to-treat): beta -0.97, 95% CI -1.67 to -0.28, p=0.006
Physical IPV among couples attending more than 75% of sessions (per-protocol): adjusted OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.21-0.94, p=0.04
Justifications for wife-beating among higher-attendance couples (per-protocol): adjusted beta -1.14, 95% CI -2.01 to -0.28, p=0.01
Economic abuse among both low- and high-adherence women (per-protocol): adjusted OR 0.31 and 0.47 respectively (p<=0.01)
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome - past-year physical and/or sexual IPV (intent-to-treat): OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.58-1.47, not significant
Physical IPV alone (intent-to-treat): OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39-1.21, not significant
Sexual IPV alone (intent-to-treat or per-protocol) - not significant
Attitudes toward a woman's ability to refuse sex - did not significantly change

key_message: In this pilot RCT in conflict-affected rural Cote d'Ivoire, adding gender dialogue sessions for women and their male partners to an economic savings program did not significantly reduce the primary outcome of past-year physical/sexual IPV in the full intent-to-treat sample - but it did significantly reduce economic abuse and acceptance of wife-beating, and among couples who attended more than 75% of sessions together, physical IPV itself was significantly reduced. This dose-response pattern (higher attendance leading to real violence reduction) suggests the gender-dialogue component can work, but only when male partners are genuinely engaged, not just nominally exposed to the programme.
limitations: Self-reported IPV is subject to social desirability and disclosure bias in both directions (under- or over-reporting)
Participants, facilitators, and researchers were not blinded to treatment status, and treatment/control groups shared villages, creating a risk of contamination biasing results toward the null
Small pilot scale (24 villages); the authors call for larger-scale replication
Per-protocol (attendance-based) findings are not randomised comparisons and may reflect self-selection - couples who attend more may differ systematically from those who don't

intervention_name: SASA!: community mobilisation intervention to prevent violence against women and reduce HIV risk

population.sample_size_detail: 8 communities in Kampala, Uganda (4 intervention, 4 control), pair-matched; repeated cross-sectional random samples of community members aged 18-49 at baseline (n=1583) and 4-year follow-up (n=2532)

intervention.description: SASA! community mobilisation intervention: local activists and staged phases (Start, Awareness, Support, Action) working to shift community norms around power, gender, and violence, aiming to reduce IPV and HIV risk
intervention.duration: Implemented 2007-2012; outcomes assessed approximately 4 years post-implementation via repeated cross-sectional surveys

study_design_full: Pair-matched, cluster-randomised controlled trial; 8 communities (4 intervention, 4 control) in Kampala, Uganda; repeated cross-sectional surveys at baseline and 4-year follow-up, adjusted cluster-level intention-to-treat analysis

effect.direction: Significant improvements in attitudes/social norms and community response to violence, and directionally lower past-year physical and sexual IPV, though the IPV prevalence reductions themselves did not reach statistical significance
worked_for: Social acceptance of IPV among women: adjusted risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.79
Acceptance that a woman can refuse sex - women: adjusted risk ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.07-1.52; men: adjusted risk ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.00-1.70
Women experiencing violence in intervention communities were more likely to receive supportive community responses
Past-year sexual concurrency reported by men: adjusted risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.36-0.91
did_not_work_for: Past-year physical IPV among women: adjusted risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.16-1.39 (a 52% lower point estimate, but the confidence interval crosses 1 - not statistically significant)
Past-year sexual IPV among women: adjusted risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.33-1.72 - not statistically significant
Social acceptance of IPV among men: adjusted risk ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.01-1.15 - large point estimate but not statistically significant given the very wide confidence interval

key_message: SASA!, one of the most widely replicated community-mobilisation interventions to prevent violence against women (now delivered in 15+ countries), significantly shifted community attitudes toward IPV and toward women's right to refuse sex in this landmark Kampala cluster-RCT, and community members became more supportive when women disclosed violence - but the directional reductions in past-year physical and sexual IPV prevalence itself, while substantial in size (e.g. a 52% lower point estimate for physical IPV), did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting the small number of clusters (8) relative to how entrenched these behaviours are. This pattern - attitude and norm change outpacing measurable violence reduction within a single trial's timeframe - recurs across several other studies in this dataset.
limitations: Small number of clusters (8 communities total) limits statistical power/precision, especially for the primary violence-prevalence outcomes
Repeated cross-sectional (not longitudinal individual-level) design measures community-level change, not individual trajectories
Possible undetected contamination between intervention and control communities despite geographical buffers, given the small overall study area and the socially diffusive nature of the intervention
Self-reported attitudes and violence are subject to social desirability/reporting bias, which may differ by study arm and sex
External programming interruptions and population mobility during the study period may have limited or diluted intervention exposure among respondents

intervention_name: Zomba cash transfer programme (conditional and unconditional cash transfers for schooling)

population.sample_size_detail: 2907 baseline schoolgirls + 889 baseline dropouts across 176 enumeration areas randomised to conditional CT, unconditional CT, or control

intervention.description: Monthly cash transfers to never-married adolescent girls/young women and their households over 2 school years; conditional arm required 80% school attendance, unconditional arm had no conditions; household amount $4-10/month, girl's amount $1-5/month, both randomly varied

study_design_full: Cluster-randomised controlled trial; 176 enumeration areas in Zomba district randomised to conditional cash transfer, unconditional cash transfer, or control arms

effect.direction: Effective for girls enrolled in school at baseline - large reductions in HIV and HSV-2 prevalence at 18 months; no significant effect for girls who had already dropped out of school at baseline, and no significant difference between conditional and unconditional sub-arms
worked_for: Girls enrolled in school at baseline: HIV prevalence 1.2% (intervention) vs 3.0% (control), adjusted OR 0.36 (95% CI 0.14-0.91)
Girls enrolled in school at baseline: HSV-2 prevalence 0.7% vs 3.0%, adjusted OR 0.24 (95% CI 0.09-0.65)
Secondary outcomes: reduced early marriage and pregnancy, increased school enrolment
did_not_work_for: Girls who were already out of school at baseline (no significant effect on HIV/HSV-2)
No significant difference in effect between conditional vs unconditional transfer arms

key_message: A two-year cash transfer programme tied to school enrolment - with no direct focus on sexual behaviour change - nearly halved HIV and HSV-2 prevalence among adolescent girls who were in school at baseline, while also reducing early marriage, showing that addressing the economic and educational drivers of girls' vulnerability can meaningfully reduce violence-adjacent and health harms; it did not help girls who had already left school.
limitations: No baseline HIV/HSV-2 data, so incidence between arms cannot be directly compared, only prevalence at 18 months
Low absolute number of biological events (7 HIV cases in the combined intervention group vs 17 in control) means effect estimates should be interpreted cautiously
Not powered to detect differences between conditional and unconditional cash transfer sub-arms
Short 2-year intervention period; durability of effects beyond the transfer period unknown
Restricted to never-married girls/young women aged 13-22 in one district of Malawi; findings may not generalise elsewhere

intervention_name: Good School Toolkit (whole-school violence prevention intervention)

population.sample_size_detail: 3820 of 4138 randomly sampled students (92.4%) across 42 primary schools (21 intervention, 21 waitlist control)

intervention.description: Good School Toolkit - a complex behavioural, whole-school intervention developed by Ugandan NGO Raising Voices, designed to change school culture and reduce corporal punishment/violence from staff toward students

study_design_full: Two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial; 42 primary schools in Luwero District randomised to intervention (21) or waitlist control (21), cross-sectional baseline (2012) and endline (2014) student surveys

effect.direction: Effective - large reduction in past-week physical violence from school staff to students at 18 months
worked_for: Past-week physical violence from school staff: 31.0% (intervention) vs 48.7% (control), odds ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.26-0.64, p<0.0001)

key_message: A whole-school behaviour-change intervention - not targeted at individual perpetrators but at changing school culture and governance - cut the prevalence of physical violence from teachers/staff to primary school students by around 60% within 18 months, showing that structural/institutional violence prevention approaches can work at scale even without direct disciplinary sanctions.
limitations: Could not mask school staff/students to intervention assignment, given the nature of the intervention
Possible contamination between arms noted at one point during the trial (would bias effect towards the null, so true effect may be larger)
Relies on students' self-reported experiences of violence, which may be subject to reporting/recall bias
Single district in Uganda; generalisability to other settings and age profiles may vary
434 children were referred to child protective services based on survey disclosures - an important ethical/safeguarding consideration for future replications

intervention_name: Caregiver support curriculum added to adolescent girls' life skills programme (Journeys of Empowerment)

population.age_range: Girls 10-14 years; caregivers of participating girls
population.sex: Girls only (girls' outcomes); caregivers (mixed) received the added intervention
population.sample_size_detail: 869 adolescent girls and 764 caregivers across 35 clusters (18 treatment, 17 wait-list control) in South Kivu

intervention.description: Adolescent girls in both arms received 32 life skills sessions; caregivers in the treatment arm additionally received 13 complementary caregiver sessions on emotional, parental and social support skills

study_design_full: Two-arm, single-blinded, cluster-randomised controlled trial; 35 clusters (18 treatment, 17 wait-list control) in a humanitarian/conflict-affected setting in South Kivu, DRC

effect.direction: No effect on girls' exposure to sexual violence or other measured violence outcomes; improved caregivers' supportive parenting behaviours
worked_for: Caregivers' supportive parenting behaviours (improved in treatment arm)
Protocol adherence (attending sessions) was associated with better outcomes
did_not_work_for: Girls' self-reported exposure to sexual violence in the past 12 months (primary outcome): adjusted OR 0.95 (95% CI 0.65-1.37) - no significant difference
Secondary violence outcomes for girls (physical/emotional violence, transactional sex, child marriage) - no significant differences

key_message: Adding a caregiver-focused curriculum to an adolescent girls' life skills programme improved caregivers' parenting behaviours, but this did not translate into a measurable reduction in girls' exposure to sexual or other violence over 12 months in this conflict-affected setting - suggesting that caregiver-only add-ons may need to be paired with more direct or frequent engagement to shift girls' violence outcomes.
limitations: Possible within-village contamination since both treatment and control groups existed in some villages, which would bias results toward the null
All outcomes were self-reported and subject to disclosure bias, though ACASI was used to reduce social desirability bias
Conducted in a conflict-affected humanitarian setting; findings may not generalise to other populations in the region
Only 12-month follow-up; longer-term effects unknown

intervention_name: Skhokho holistic school intervention (Life Orientation curriculum plus caregiver-teen family programme)

population.sample_size_detail: 3756 Grade 8 learners at baseline (61.8% of total), 3411 (90.8%) provided endline data, across 24 schools

intervention.description: Three-arm trial: (1) no-intervention control, (2) schools' package - a Life Orientation curriculum workbook plus teacher training, (3) combined schools' package plus a family package - caregiver/teen workshops supported by clubs in year 2

study_design_full: Pragmatic, three-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial across 24 state schools in Grade 8 classes; under-powered by enrolment shortfalls

effect.direction: Primary IPV/rape outcomes not statistically significant but consistently trended toward protection; several secondary violence-related outcomes significantly improved
worked_for: Trend of lower incidence of any/severe IPV and non-partner rape perpetration across both intervention arms vs control (not statistically significant, aIRR ~0.84 for girls)
Reduced childhood trauma, bullying, and more equitable gender attitudes among boys (schools arm)
Reduced depression and bullying among girls
Reduced transactional sex and fewer pregnancies reported by girls in the family's arm
Caregivers reported improved communication, lower parenting stress, and less own IPV exposure
did_not_work_for: Primary outcomes (incidence of physical/sexual IPV, severe IPV, non-partner rape) did not reach statistical significance - study was substantially under-powered

key_message: A low-cost, holistic school intervention combining a classroom Life Orientation curriculum with an optional family/caregiver workshop showed a consistent (though not statistically significant, due to under-powering) trend toward reduced dating and sexual violence, alongside significant improvements in bullying, depression, gender attitudes and caregiver-reported outcomes - suggesting real promise that warrants a fully powered replication.
limitations: Substantially under-powered - fewer learners contributed to the primary outcome analysis than planned, partly due to caregiver/learner consent rates
Randomisation occurred prior to recruitment, which may have influenced who consented to participate
No fidelity data for the classroom curriculum - design reflects the impact of making materials available rather than curriculum delivery itself (a pragmatic trial)
Only around a third of caregivers and learners attended all four family intervention sessions
Self-reported violence perpetration/experience may be affected by honesty and social desirability, particularly for boys

intervention_name: SAFE (Sexual violence-free community mobilisation + group sessions) programme

population.sample_size_detail: 2,666 currently-married women (15-29) and 930 men (18-35) at baseline across 19 slum clusters in Dhaka; 2,670 women and 1,026 men at endline

intervention.description: Three-arm cluster trial nested on a base of community mobilisation and one-stop service centres: (A) base only (control), (B) base + 13 female-only group sessions on gender, rights, SRHR and violence prevention, (C) base + combined female and male group sessions

study_design_full: Three-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial across 19 urban slum clusters in Dhaka, Bangladesh (March 2012-October 2013)

effect.direction: No significant overall reduction in past-year IPV among women 15-29, but a significant reduction in physical IPV against adolescent wives (15-19) in the arm combining male and female group sessions
worked_for: 21% risk reduction in physical IPV against adolescent girls (15-19) in the combined male+female group sessions arm (C)
Consistent, though not statistically significant, reductions in sexual violence across both intervention arms
did_not_work_for: No significant reduction in physical, sexual or economic IPV for the full sample of women aged 15-29

key_message: Adding structured group sessions on gender, rights and violence to community mobilisation and service provision did not shift IPV for the wider population of women, but engaging husbands alongside wives was linked to a meaningful drop in physical violence against the youngest, most vulnerable wives - underscoring the value of involving men in prevention programming.
limitations: Short follow-up period (about 4 months after the intervention ended)
High population turnover/out-migration in slum settings
Much lower male than female survey coverage (about 15% vs 51%), limiting power for male-reported outcomes
Possible social desirability bias in self-reported violence
Contamination between geographically close clusters was not measured

intervention_name: Comprehensive school support for orphan girls (fees, uniforms, supplies, teacher mentors)
citation: Hallfors, Cho, Rusakaniko, Iritani, Mapfumo & Halpern (2011)

population.age_range: Grade 6 orphan girls, mean age 12.2 years
population.sample_size_detail: 329 orphan girls in Grade 6 across 25 primary schools (184 intervention, 145 control) in rural Manicaland province, followed over 3 annual survey waves

intervention.description: Comprehensive support to keep orphan girls in school: payment of school fees, uniforms and supplies, plus a trained female teacher-mentor who monitored attendance and provided support; all schools (intervention and control) also received a universal school feeding programme

study_design_full: School-randomised controlled trial across 25 primary schools in rural eastern Zimbabwe (13 intervention, 12 control), with 3 annual survey waves

effect.direction: Large reductions in school dropout and child marriage, alongside improved school bonding and gender attitudes
worked_for: 82% reduction in school dropout among intervention girls vs control
63% reduction in marriage rates
Greater school bonding, more equitable gender attitudes, and greater concern about the consequences of sex reported by intervention girls
did_not_work_for: Self-reported sexual intercourse was not reliably reduced (authors note self-report data on this outcome is unreliable)

key_message: Comprehensive economic and social support to keep orphan adolescent girls in school - covering fees, supplies and a caring teacher-mentor - produced large reductions in dropout and child marriage, suggesting school-retention support is a promising indirect pathway for reducing girls' HIV and violence risk.
limitations: Self-reported sexual intercourse data considered unreliable
Findings specific to a rural, orphan-girl population in eastern Zimbabwe and may not generalise
Support and monitoring became inconsistent once girls transitioned to secondary school

intervention_name: Adolescent Girls Initiative-Kenya (AGI-K) multisectoral cash-plus programme
citation: Austrian, Soler-Hampejsek, Kangwana, Wado, Abuya & Maluccio (2021)

population.sample_size_detail: 2,390 girls in Kibera (urban informal settlement, individually randomised) and 2,147 girls in Wajir (rural pastoralist county, cluster-randomised) at baseline; 2,190 and 1,909 respectively at 2-year follow-up

intervention.description: Two-year, four-arm 'cash plus' trial nesting a violence-prevention community-dialogue component with additional layers: (1) violence prevention alone, (2) + education conditional cash transfer, (3) + health/life-skills girls' groups, (4) + wealth-creation/financial-literacy training

study_design_full: Multisectoral randomised trial with 4 nested arms; individually randomised in Kibera (urban) and cluster-randomised in Wajir (rural); no pure no-intervention control arm

effect.direction: Multisectoral cash-plus arms reduced violence in the urban site but showed little effect in the rural site
worked_for: Violence experience fell 4-9 percentage points across arms in Kibera (from a 42% baseline), reaching statistical significance in the arms adding education and health components
did_not_work_for: No significant violence-reduction effects in Wajir after correcting for multiple comparisons, likely reflecting a much lower baseline violence rate (3.8%)
Gender-attitude effects were mixed and modest across sites

key_message: A multisectoral 'cash plus' approach - combining violence-prevention dialogues with education, health and economic-empowerment components - reduced girls' violence experience in an urban informal settlement, but context strongly moderated effectiveness, with little detectable effect in a rural pastoralist setting with a much lower baseline violence rate.
limitations: No arm isolates the violence-prevention component alone, so its independent effect cannot be assessed
Different levels of intervention exposure across the nested arms complicate comparisons
Possible spillover/contamination between arms in the densely-populated Kibera site
Limited statistical power for rarer long-term outcomes such as pregnancy and marriage

intervention_name: Good School Toolkit (whole-school violence prevention intervention) - sex-disaggregated analysis
citation: Devries, Knight, Allen, Parkes, Kyegombe & Naker (2017)

population.sample_size_detail: 3,820 students interviewed at endline (92.3% retention) across 42 primary schools (21 intervention, 21 control) in Luwero District, Uganda; same trial and endline survey as Devries et al. (2015), re-analysed by sex

intervention.description: Same whole-school Good School Toolkit intervention as Devries et al. (2015) - a complex, six-step programme fostering change in school operational culture (respect, power dynamics, teaching methods, accountability, non-violent discipline), delivered by trained staff and student 'protagonists' - here re-analysed to test whether effectiveness differed for boys vs girls

study_design_full: Secondary, sex-disaggregated analysis of the same two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial reported in Devries et al. (2015), across 42 primary schools in Luwero District, Uganda (wait-list control)

effect.direction: The Toolkit reduced violence for both sexes, but effects were significantly stronger for boys than girls, with a non-significant signal of increased sexual violence reports among girls
worked_for: Past-week violence from staff and/or peers reduced for both boys (aOR 0.34) and girls (aOR 0.55)
Injuries from staff violence reduced for both boys (aOR 0.36) and girls (aOR 0.51), with a larger effect in boys over the past term (p<0.0001)
No significant sex difference in reduction of peer emotional or physical violence
did_not_work_for: Past-week staff physical violence reduction was significantly weaker for girls (aOR 0.45) than boys (aOR 0.33), a significant sex interaction (p=0.033)
Borderline (non-significant) increase in reports of sexual violence for girls specifically

key_message: Re-analysing the Good School Toolkit trial by sex shows the intervention reduced violence for both boys and girls, but its protective effect was consistently weaker for girls - with a worrying, if non-significant, signal of increased sexual violence reports among girls - suggesting whole-school interventions may need stronger, explicit mechanisms to engage and protect girls specifically.
limitations: Exploratory sex-disaggregated analysis with limited statistical power to detect interaction effects
Single-item outcome measures subject to measurement error
Multiple statistical comparisons increase the risk of chance findings
All measures are self-report; sexual violence is likely under-reported
